rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a pitchable story and a pretty trap. Its best line is the discipline in “Names of the three insurers... this is a blocking gap,” while B wanders into unsupported heat with “Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?” A gives the founder four usable lanes and the missing proof for each; B has some good instincts, then tries to sell questions the facts have not earned.
gaps_in_A: “Health Insurers Start Covering Meditation Apps” overgeneralizes from three unnamed national insurers to the whole payer market; it needs payer names or comparable deals before that plural earns its keep.

“The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving” is a little grand for one self-reported anxiety study among regular users; the clinical claim needs the instrument, cohort definition, and journal tier before it carries that weight.

“The prevailing belief in tech-health press is that independent university execution neutralizes industry funding” is asserted, not supplied. The integrity angle is good, but that media-psychology claim is decoration.
gaps_in_B: “default benefit for 25 million Americans” invents both “default” and “Americans.” The update says covered benefit for an estimated 25 million members, which is not the same thing.

“Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?” is a sharper headline than the facts can support. There is no evidence these plans are replacing therapy or dodging parity obligations.

“What Calm actually gets paid when 25 million people get it for free” makes undisclosed revenue terms the story, but no terms exist in the update. That is a reporting question, not a founder-ready angle.

The study angle asks for sample size and dropout rate, good, but misses two killer qualifiers: what counts as “regular users” and what instrument measured anxiety. Without those, the 18% number is floating.
